# Evaluating $\oint_{|z|=1} \log(z)\,dz$

## Setting Up the Problem

The key challenge is that $\log(z)$ has a **branch point at $z=0$**, which lies inside the unit circle, so $\log(z)$ is not single-valued on the contour. I'll parameterize the circle and use a continuous branch along the path.

**Parameterization:** Let $z = e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta: 0 \to 2\pi$ (counterclockwise). Along this path, I define a continuous branch:
$$\log(z) = i\theta, \qquad dz = i\,e^{i\theta}\,d\theta$$

## Computing the Integral

$$\oint_{|z|=1} \log(z)\,dz = \int_0^{2\pi} i\theta \;\cdot\; i\,e^{i\theta}\,d\theta = -\int_0^{2\pi} \theta\, e^{i\theta}\,d\theta$$

**Integration by parts:** Let $u = \theta$, $dv = e^{i\theta}d\theta$, so $du = d\theta$, $v = \dfrac{e^{i\theta}}{i}$.

$$\int_0^{2\pi} \theta\,e^{i\theta}\,d\theta = \left[\frac{\theta\,e^{i\theta}}{i}\right]_0^{2\pi} - \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{e^{i\theta}}{i}\,d\theta$$

Evaluating each term:

| Term | Evaluation |
|---|---|
| $\left[\dfrac{\theta e^{i\theta}}{i}\right]_0^{2\pi}$ | $\dfrac{2\pi\,e^{2\pi i}-0}{i} = \dfrac{2\pi}{i} = -2\pi i$ |
| $\dfrac{1}{i}\left[\dfrac{e^{i\theta}}{i}\right]_0^{2\pi}$ | $\dfrac{1}{i}\cdot\dfrac{e^{2\pi i}-e^{0}}{i} = \dfrac{1-1}{i^2} = 0$ |

Therefore:
$$\int_0^{2\pi} \theta\,e^{i\theta}\,d\theta = -2\pi i$$

And the original integral:
$$\oint_{|z|=1} \log(z)\,dz = -(-2\pi i) = 2\pi i$$

## Verification via Antiderivative

An antiderivative of $\log(z)$ is $F(z) = z\log z - z$ (since $F'(z) = \log z$). Traversing the unit circle once, $z$ returns to $1$, but $\log z$ gains $2\pi i$:

$$F\big|_{\text{end}} - F\big|_{\text{start}} = \big[1\cdot(2\pi i)-1\big] - \big[1\cdot 0 - 1\big] = 2\pi i - 1 + 1 = 2\pi i \;\checkmark$$

This jump of $2\pi i$ reflects the multivalued nature of the logarithm encircling its branch point.

$$\boxed{2\pi i}$$
